etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English tape, tappe, from Old English tæppa, tæppe (“ribbon, tape”). Probably akin to Old Frisian tapia (“to pull, rip, tear”), Middle Low German tappen, tāpen (“to grab, pull, rip, tear, snatch”), Middle High German zāfen, zāven (“to pull, tear”).

definitions.definition: Flexible material in a roll with a sticky surface on one or both sides; adhesive tape.
Thin and flat paper, plastic or similar flexible material, usually produced in the form of a roll.
Finishing tape, stretched across a track to mark the end of a race.
Magnetic or optical recording media in a roll; videotape or audio tape.

quote.text: So we went around the corner, looked in the garbage, and, boom, there's about 16 of the tapes he didn't like!

definitions.definition: (informal, by extension) Any video or audio recording, regardless of the method used to produce it.

quote.citation: 2018 August 18, Susan Edelman, New York Post:
quote.text: “It was one of the most severe beatings they’ve seen on tape,” an FDNY insider said, recalling the reaction by brass who viewed video of the bloody fisticuffs.

definitions.definition: (informal) An unthinking, patterned response triggered by a particular stimulus.
(trading, from ticker tape) The series of prices at which a financial instrument trades.
(ice hockey) The wrapping of the primary puck-handling surface of a hockey stick
(printing, historical) A strong flexible band rotating on pulleys for directing the sheets in a printing machine.
(possible, obsolete, UK, slang) Liquor, alcoholic drink, especially gin or brandy. (Especially in prison slang or among domestic servants and women.)

quote.text: Madam Gin has been christened by as many names as a German princess : every petty chandler's shop will sell you Sky-blue, and every night-cellar furnish you with Holland tape, three yards a penny. Nor can I see the difference […]

quote.text: […]  who is now puffing his pipe and sipping his grog, as unconcerned as a Dutch fiddler at a merry-making, has no business here selling his cheese and candles in the day-time, and his yards of tape in the evening:  […]  and now then for the tape-shop.  […]

definitions.definition: Clipping of red tape (“time-consuming bureaucratic procedures”).

quote.citation: 1923, Henry C. Clark, Departmental Practice, Admission of Attorneys, Etc, page 7:
quote.text: [When dealing with the] Federal Government, "red tape" is unavoidable. Perseverance, good humor and thoroughness will almost invariably cut through the "tape” or lead to the proper official where courteous and attentive treatment will be received.

quote.text: He was going to cut through the tape and ship this Army stuff straight to France.
